pronunciation.body:
The conventional ​scholarly reading of the ‌name is **/ˈbajaˌmi/** — ‌an approximate phonemic rendering ​based on English-language ​ethnographic sources[^1].

For the ​English-speaking reader, the closest ​approximation is: 'BYE-ah-meh' — ​stress the first ‌syllable, keep the vowels ​open, and avoid a ​long English 'ee' at ‌the end.

Because ​the name was transmitted ‌orally across several language ​groups, precise phonetic reconstruction ‌is not possible. ​The Gamilaraay form **Baayami** ​is sometimes pronounced with ​a longer first vowel, ​while the Wiradjuri ​**Baiame** often carries stress ‌on the first syllable ​and a lighter middle ‌syllable.

Baiame is ​a simpler restoration because ‌the ASCII form *baiame* ​already represents the same ‌conventional phonemic sequence; ​no stress mark, length ‌mark, or distinctive letter ​is required to recover ​the spoken name ‌as it appears in ‌standard scholarly sources.

Because ‌Baiame belongs to an ​oral tradition, the ​reconstructed pronunciation offered here ‌is a scholarly romanization ​rather than a phonetic ​record of a ‌living speaker. The sounds ​of the original language ​include phonemes that English ‌does not distinguish, ​and early recorders used ‌inconsistent English-based spellings. PuniCodex ​therefore treats the capitalized ​scholarly form **Baiame** ​as the reference spelling, ​while noting that the ‌ASCII form represents the ‌same romanized sequence. ​This is why the ‌name is a plain ​restoration: the restoration recovers ​the proper-noun convention ‌of the name without ‌adding a diacritic or ‌special letter that the ‌original ASCII string ​could not carry.

domains.body:
Baiame's ​domain is ‌creation itself: ‌the land, ​the sky, ​the living ​creatures, ​and the ​moral law ‌that binds ​them together. ​As Sky ‌Father ​he watches ‌from above; ​as Maker ‌he is ​the source ​of ​all physical ​and social ​form. His ‌cult is ​not ‌one of ​daily worship ‌but of ​memory and ‌obligation: the ​people ‌keep his ​law, tend ​his country, ‌and pass ‌his stories ‌to ​the next ​generation.

The ‌domain of ​**Baiame** is ​understood within ‌the ​broader Aboriginal ​religious landscape ‌as both ​a specific ‌functional sphere ​and ​a node ​in a ​network of ‌creator ancestors, ‌sky beings, ​and ‌country. Daramulum, ​often identified ​as his ‌son, mediates ‌between the ‌Sky ‌Father and ​human communities, ‌especially in ​initiation. Birrahgnooloo ​(or Birran ​gnulu) ‌appears in ​some traditions ​as a ​complementary earth ‌or ​fertility figure. ​The restoration ​**Baiame** therefore ‌names not ​only a ‌mythic ​person but ‌a living ​field of ‌cultural responsibility: ‌land care, ​ceremony, ​language, and ​protocol continue ​to define ‌what the ‌name means ​today.

mythology.body:
The ​central mythic ‌complex ‌around Baiame ​is ​the ​creation of ​the ​world and ‌the ​establishment of ​law. ‌After making ​the ‌land, the ​animals, ‌and ​the people, ​Baiame ​gave the ​first ​people their ‌languages, ​countries, and ‌kinship ​systems. He ‌then ​withdrew ‌to the ​sky, ‌leaving his ​son ​Daramulum to ‌teach ‌initiation and ‌mediate ​between heaven ​and ‌earth.

​The narrative ​of ‌**Baiame** participates ​in ​the larger ‌mythic ​program of ‌Aboriginal ​Australia: to ​explain ​the ​origin of ‌country, ‌the structure ​of ‌society, and ​the ​responsibilities that ‌bind ‌people to ‌the ‌land. ​Because these ‌stories ​are held ​by ​traditional custodians, ‌published ​versions are ​summaries ​rather than ‌authoritative ​teachings. ​Modern readers ​must ‌distinguish between ​the ‌public scholarly ​record ‌and the ​restricted ‌sacred knowledge ‌that ​remains ​the property ​of ​initiated men ‌in ‌the relevant ​nations.

cultural-legacy.body:
Baiame remains ​a powerful symbol of ‌Aboriginal sovereignty over ‌country and culture. His ​name appears in ​place names, in ​rock art and stencil ​sites, and in ​contemporary Aboriginal art and ‌literature. The Emu ​in the Sky is ​now widely recognised ‌as one of the ​best-known Aboriginal astronomical ‌traditions, referenced in ​education, planetarium shows, and ‌cultural-tourism interpretation.

At ​the same time, Aboriginal ​custodians have rightly ​insisted that Baiame's sacred ​aspects — especially ​those connected with men's ‌law and initiation ​— are not ‌open-source material for casual ​adaptation. PuniCodex presents ‌only the publicly documented, ​scholarly record and ‌directs readers to AIATSIS ​and to the ‌relevant Aboriginal communities for ​authoritative teachings.

Today ​Baiame appears in ‌Aboriginal Australian art, storytelling, ‌environmental education, and ‌cultural tourism, always under ​the guidance of ​the communities who hold ‌the name. Bark ​paintings, rock-art sites, dance ​cycles, and welcome-to-country ‌ceremonies keep the ​figure present in public ​life, while restricted ‌knowledge remains within appropriate ​kin and ceremonial ‌contexts. The name also ​serves as a ​reminder that the ​domain-name system was built ​on ASCII assumptions ‌that erase the proper-noun ‌conventions of many ​Indigenous languages; restoring **Baiame** ‌as a flagship ​temple is one small ​act of acknowledging ‌that erasure and ‌preserving the scholarly citation ‌form for future ‌reference.

archaeology.body:
The material ​record of ‌Baiame-related belief includes ‌stone arrangements, ​bora (initiation) grounds, ​rock engravings, and ​rock shelters ​across Wiradjuri and ​Gamilaraay countries ‌in New South ​Wales. Notable ​sites include Baiame ‌Cave near Milbrodale ​in the ‌Hunter Valley, which ​contains a ‌large painted figure ​sometimes identified ​with Baiame, and ​numerous carved and ​painted emus ​that reference the ‌Emu in ​the Sky. These ‌sites are ​protected under Aboriginal ‌cultural-heritage law and ​are best ‌understood in consultation ​with traditional ‌custodians.

The material ​record associated ​with Baiame includes ‌rock-art galleries, ceremonial ‌grounds, waterholes, ‌and landscape features ​that are ​identified by custodians ‌as the ​work or residence ​of the ancestor. ‌These sites ​are not mere ​archaeological deposits; ‌they are living ​places whose ‌significance is renewed ​through ritual ​and custodial practice. ​Access to many ​sites is ‌restricted by Aboriginal ‌protocol, and ​the public scholarly ‌record therefore ​represents only the ​outer layer of ‌a much ‌deeper body of ‌knowledge.

syncretism.body:
Early ​colonial ‌observers ‌sometimes ​compared ​Baiame ​to the ​Christian ​God, ‌and ​some ​recorded ‌traditions ​show ‌signs ​of ‌post-contact ​reinterpretation. Modern ​scholarship, ​led ​by ​Berndt ‌and ​Berndt ‌and ​by ‌AIATSIS, ​treats ‌Baiame as ​a ‌specifically ​Aboriginal ​Sky ‌Father ‌whose ‌identity ​is ​tied ‌to ​country, kinship, ​and ‌initiation ​rather ​than ‌to ​any ‌universal ​deity. ​He ​is ​not interchangeable ‌with ‌the ​biblical ‌creator, ​and ​each ‌nation ‌retains ‌its ‌own ​protocols for ‌how ​his ​name ​and ‌stories ​may ​be ​used.[^1]

‌Kindred ​figures ​in the ​PuniCodex ‌cross-tradition ​index ‌include ​[[ahuramazda|AhuraMazdā]], ‌[[audhumla|Auðhumla]], ​[[bunjil|Bunjil]], ‌[[izanagi|Izanagi]], ‌[[jagannatha|Jagannātha]], ​and ​[[oduduwa|Odùduwà]], each ​linked ​through ‌creator ‌/ ​cosmogonic.

overview.body:
**Baiame** (*baiame*) ​— Sky ‌Father, Creator ‌· The ​eaglehawk father ​of southeast ​Australia — ​belongs to ​the Aboriginal ‌tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Sky Father, ‌Creator". The ​name means ‌"The maker"[^1].

​**Baiame** is ​the great ​creator and ​Sky Father ​of several ‌Aboriginal nations ​of south-eastern ‌Australia, above ​all the ‌Wiradjuri and ​the Gamilaraay/Euahlayi. ‌He made ​the land, ‌the animals, ​and the ​people, and ‌then gave ‌them the ‌laws, kinship ​systems, and ​initiation ceremonies ‌by which ​they still ​live. After ‌the work ​of creation ​he withdrew ‌to the ​sky, where ‌he remains ​as a ​remote but ​watchful ancestor, ​his presence ‌felt in ‌the Milky ​Way, in ‌the flight ​of the ​emu, and ‌in the ‌sound of ‌the bullroarer ‌at initiation.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ​scholarly spelling ​**Baiame** and ​serves its ‌temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/baiame/). ​The displayed ​form is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ​computed from ​the displayed ‌form itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*baiame* contains ‌the same ​letters: no ‌recovered diacritics ‌or special ​encoding is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is consistent ‌citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, and ​cultural context[^3].

the-name.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives ​for this ​name; ​**Baiame** ​is a ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​of the ​reconstructed ‌spoken ​form. Etymologically ‌the ​name ‌means "The ​maker"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ​**Baiame** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. The ​plain ‌ASCII ​form *baiame* ‌contains ​the ‌same letters, ​so ​no ‌lost diacritics ‌or ‌encoding transition ​is ​claimed. ‌The editorial ​work ​is ‌to fix ​one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization ​and provenance, ​and ​keep ​the original ‌evidence ‌visible. ​The displayed ‌form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a ‌description computed ‌from ‌the ​displayed form ‌itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**b** ​→ **B** ​— ​Same, ‌capitalized
- **a** ​→ ​**a** — ​Same
- ‌**i** ​→ **i** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**a** → ​**a** ‌— ‌Same
- **m** ​→ ​**m** ​— Same
- ​**e** ‌→ ‌**e** — ​Same

original-script.body:
No ​indigenous ‌writing system ‌is ​securely ​attested for ​individual ​aboriginal ​names. The ‌form ​shown ​is ‌a modern ​scholarly ‌transliteration.[^1]

​The form ‌**Baiame** ​is ​therefore ​a scholarly ​transliteration ​rather ‌than an ​attested ‌ancient ​spelling; it ‌encodes ​the ‌reconstructed ​sound of ‌the ​name ​for modern ‌use, ‌and ‌no ​mark in ​it ‌is ​decorative.

Baiame ​belongs ‌to ​an oral ​tradition ‌that ​had ‌no pre-contact ​writing ​system. ​The name ​first ‌enters ‌the written ​record ‌in ​nineteenth-century ​ethnographies. PuniCodex ‌therefore ‌restores ‌it as ‌**Baiame**, ​the ‌conventional ​capitalized romanization, ​rather ​than ‌as an ​'original ​script' ​in the ‌strict ​sense. ​The ​conventional spelling ‌**baiame** ​is ‌the scholarly ​citation ‌form ​used ‌in Australian ‌Indigenous ​studies; ​the lowercase ​form ​*baiame* ‌differs only ‌in ​capitalization.

meditation.body:
Baiame ​asks the ‌modern reader ‌to think ​about creation ​as responsibility. ​The world ​is ​not a ‌finished product ​handed to ​humanity; it ‌is a ​country made ‌by ​an ancestor ‌and entrusted ​to his ​descendants. To ​speak the ​name ​Baiame is ‌therefore to ​remember a ‌covenant: the ​land, the ‌water, the ​animals, ‌and the ​sky are ‌kin, and ​the law ​that governs ‌them is ‌older ‌than any ​statute.

That ​is why ‌the restoration ​matters. The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​flattens the ​name into ‌a string ​of letters ‌with no ​memory ​of the ​languages that ​carried it. ‌The canonical ‌restoration **Baiame** ​does not ‌add ​diacritics, because ​the original ‌sources were ‌oral, but ‌it does ‌reclaim the ​capitalized, ‌scholarly citation ​form by ​which the ​figure is ‌named in ​museums, universities, ​and ​Aboriginal-studies curricula. ‌The name ​is a ​plain restoration ​not because ‌it ​is less ‌important, but ​because the ‌DNS-friendly ASCII ​form already ‌encodes the ‌same ​phonemic sequence. ​The work ​of preservation ​here is ‌cultural and ‌historical, not ​diacritical.[^1]
